channel.title: Daily Recap — 📟Tech News
channel.description: What happened in 📟Tech News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Judge blocks the FCC from reviewing ABC's licenses early
item.description:
A federal judge has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses, issuing a preliminary injunction and rejecting the agency's efforts to dismiss ABC's First Amendment lawsuit. ABC has accused the FCC of waging a retaliatory campaign against the network and violating its free speech rights.

The ruling is a significant check on the FCC's leverage over broadcasters. License reviews are normally routine, periodic affairs; an early, discretionary review of a major network's licenses — brought amid a public clash — looked to ABC like punishment for its coverage. The judge's decision keeps the review on hold while the constitutional fight plays out, and it signals that courts will scrutinize the use of licensing power as a pressure tool.

Sources

  • The Verge: Federal judge blocks the FCC from reviewing ABC's licenses early

item.title: Android developers will soon have to publish their address publicly
item.description:
Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act — but Google says the contact details will be made public worldwide, not just in the EU.

The rule is aimed at accountability: users and regulators should be able to reach the person behind an app. For solo developers and small teams, though, publishing a home address feels like a real safety risk, and the global rollout means there is no way to opt out by staying out of Europe. Expect pressure on Google to offer alternatives, such as a business address or a proxy contact, before the requirement takes effect.

Sources

  • The Verge: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly

item.title: Rockstar workers vote against union recognition
item.description:
Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games have voted against formal union recognition, with only 25 percent voting in favor of a recognition agreement. Turnout was high — 1,544 employees, or 93.2 percent of eligible workers, cast ballots — so the result is a clear verdict rather than an artifact of low participation.

The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain said Rockstar workers in the union will keep organizing even without formal recognition. The vote is a setback for game-industry unionization efforts, which have been gaining ground at other studios, and it comes as GTA VI heads toward one of the biggest entertainment launches ever. For now, Rockstar's workforce remains non-union — but the organizing campaign is not over.

Sources

  • The Verge: GTA VI developers vote against unionization

item.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here — and they can feel
item.description:
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager and has cycled through several prosthetics since. His latest is different: it is wired into the nerves in the upper part of his forearm and lets him actually feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects — the kind of everyday task, like picking up something fragile without crushing it, that earlier prosthetics made a guessing game.

The advance matters because sensation is the missing piece that has kept prosthetic hands clumsy. A hand that can feel can grip with the right force, which changes what it is useful for. As neural interfaces move from lab demos into devices people live with, the line between a prosthetic and a working hand keeps getting thinner — and for users like Davidson, the difference is not theoretical, it is the ability to hold something gently.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
  • MIT Technology Review: The Download: Better bionic hands and AI's natural-gas boom

item.title: Why GTA VI's version of Florida feels so real
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI's success rests on more than 13 years of anticipation, its lead characters, and its romantic storyline — a major factor is the sense of place. The GTA series is unmatched at re-creating the feeling of a bustling real-world location, and its Florida-inspired setting is the latest example.

What makes it work is density and specificity: a world that feels lived-in rather than merely large, with the details of a real place — its light, its sprawl, its street life — rendered closely enough that players recognize the texture of somewhere they have actually been. That craft is part of why the game has become one of the most successful entertainment launches of all time, and it is a reminder that in an era of AI-generated content, painstakingly human world-building still wins.

Sources

  • The Verge: Why GTA VI's version of Florida feels so real

item.title: Black Friday tech deals are already live
item.description:
Black Friday is not officially until tomorrow, November 27, but retailers have already dropped early deals on much of the tech The Verge recommends — and with prices rising across the board, the usual caveat applies: a good discount does not necessarily mean a historically low price.

The standouts so far: the MacBook Neo is $100 off at several retailers, with the 256GB model down to $599.99 at Amazon and Costco in all four colors. The Garmin Forerunner 265S — a favorite for runners with smaller wrists, with an OLED touchscreen and strong battery life — is down to $300, its best price of the year. And streaming is the cheapest it gets: Disney Plus, Hulu, and HBO Max are all more than 50 percent off. If you are buying, check the price history before you click — early does not always mean best.

Sources

  • The Verge: The best Black Friday deals we've already found
  • The Verge: The MacBook Neo is receiving a rare $100 discount for Black Friday
  • The Verge: The Garmin Forerunner 265S is down to $300, its best price of the year
  • The Verge: Disney Plus, Hulu, and HBO Max are all over 50 percent off for Black Friday

item.title: Amazon loses court fight, must handle recalls for 400,000+ hazardous products
item.description:
Amazon is on the hook to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after losing its latest legal battle against the US Consumer Product Safety Commission. The US District Court for the District of Maryland ruled in favor of the CPSC, which argued that Amazon is a distributor of goods — not merely a logistics provider — making it responsible for handling recall notices for dangerous products sold through its marketplace.

The ruling is a major defeat for Amazon's long-standing position that it is just a platform connecting buyers and sellers. It sets a precedent that could reshape how the company vets third-party sellers and handles product safety, and it means hundreds of thousands of customers may soon receive recall notices for items they bought on Amazon.

Sources

  • The Verge: Amazon loses its latest attempt to get out of handling more recall notices

item.title: 1Password breach exposed customer names and emails — but not passwords
item.description:
1Password disclosed that a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The company says the breach did not expose passwords or any other information stored in customer vaults, and it is unclear how many users are affected.

The incident is still serious for a password manager, whose entire business rests on trust: leaked names and emails are prime fuel for targeted phishing attempts, and attackers now know exactly who uses 1Password. Customers should be extra wary of any email claiming to be from 1Password and verify links before clicking. The company has not said how the attacker got in or how long the access lasted.

Sources

  • The Verge: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords

item.title: AI is swamping America's public records systems
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has intensified investor interest in public records, and the flood of requests is overwhelming the small-town clerks who run America's open records systems. Venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect public data, and the resulting volume of requests is landing on offices that were never staffed for it.

The strain is visible in places like Panton, Vermont — population 660 — where the town clerk juggles budgets, vendors, tax disputes, zoning, and elections alongside a growing pile of records requests during morning office hours. The story is a reminder that the AI data boom has a very human, very local cost: the public records infrastructure it feeds on is held together by a handful of people in wood-frame town halls.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: AI is straining America’s open records systems

item.title: Data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
item.description:
The AI boom's appetite for electricity is driving a surge in natural gas power in the United States. Just 18 months after MIT Technology Review warned that AI could keep the country dependent on natural gas, the prediction has been borne out again and again: data centers need enormous amounts of reliable power, and gas plants are being built to supply it.

While it is technically possible to meet rising electricity demand with renewables, the speed and scale of data center growth has made gas the default answer in practice. The trend has major implications for US climate goals, since every new gas plant locks in decades of emissions — and the buildout shows no sign of slowing as AI infrastructure spending continues.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

item.title: Google patented an AI-generated personalized video channel — and it sounds bleak
item.description:
Google filed a patent last year for a system called My Channel, designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on what the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version — and the concept alone paints a bleak picture of where entertainment could be headed.

Instead of human creators making shows people choose to watch, My Channel imagines an endless feed of synthetic video tuned to each viewer's data profile, with ads woven in. The idea raises obvious questions about creativity, attention, and what happens to shared culture when everyone watches a different machine-generated feed. For now it remains a patent, not a product — but it shows where Google's thinking is going.

Sources

  • The Verge: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future

item.title: WhatsApp finally adds scheduled messages for its 3 billion users
item.description:
WhatsApp is rolling out scheduled messages, letting users pick a time to send a message in advance — in both private conversations and group chats. Meta says it's one of the most requested features, and with 3 billion users, the rollout reaches an enormous audience. Most other messaging platforms have offered scheduling for years, so WhatsApp is catching up rather than breaking new ground.

Still, for the world's most popular messaging app, the addition is genuinely useful: no more waking friends with a 2 a.m. thought, no more forgetting a birthday message. It's a small quality-of-life upgrade that will quietly change how a huge share of the planet texts.

Sources

  • The Verge: WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send

item.title: Army detonates 9,700 pounds of explosive material in Iowa; EPA reports no airborne lead
item.description:
The US Army conducted a controlled detonation of more than 9,700 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke rising several stories high.

The EPA reported "zero" airborne lead following the blast, a key concern given lead azide's toxicity. The episode highlights the ongoing challenge of safely disposing of aging military explosives — and the scale of the stockpiles the Army is still working through.

Sources

  • The Verge: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa

item.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets
item.description:
A federal jury in New York has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, closing a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of taking source code and proprietary technology from several American companies, including T-Mobile and Cisco.

The verdict is a major win for US prosecutors and lands amid the long-running confrontation between Washington and Huawei, which has already been restricted from US networks and supply chains on national security grounds. The finding could further harden the company's exclusion from Western markets and may influence ongoing policy debates about how aggressively the US polices alleged Chinese corporate espionage.

Sources

  • The Verge: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets

item.title: Treasury's financial crimes bureau discloses a cybersecurity incident
item.description:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Treasury Department bureau that collects and analyzes financial intelligence to fight money laundering and terrorist financing, disclosed on Tuesday that it is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.

FinCEN has not disclosed the scope of the breach or who was behind it, and the investigation is still underway. The incident is notable because of what FinCEN holds: sensitive reports from banks and other financial institutions about suspicious transactions. Until more is known, the key open questions are how much data was accessed and whether any of it was exfiltrated.

Sources

  • The Verge: US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’

item.title: Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia staff and pushes back on Trump narrative
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during his first all-hands meeting since returning to the company, according to reports from Bloomberg, The New York Times, and The Handbasket. He also attempted to distance himself from the narrative that the White House and other tech leaders helped him get his job back, reportedly telling staff that claim is "not true."

The apology and the denial suggest Huang is trying to reset the story around his return and reassert his own standing with employees, rather than letting the episode be framed as a politically brokered comeback. Details of what exactly he apologized for were not fully spelled out in the reports, but the meeting marks his first direct address to staff since the saga played out.

Sources

  • The Verge: Jensen Huang reportedly tells Nvidia staff it’s ‘not true’ Trump got him rehired

item.title: Clock running out on America's most contentious spying law
item.description:
Congress is scrambling to reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, with weeks left in the legislative session. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politico the authority could be attached to the must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) as a way to get it through.

Section 702 lets the government collect communications of foreign targets without individual warrants, and it has long drawn criticism from privacy advocates who argue it sweeps up Americans' data as well. Attaching it to the defense spending bill would be a familiar end-of-session maneuver, but it is not guaranteed: the provision's critics have fought similar riders before, and the outcome will shape US surveillance law for years.

Sources

  • The Verge: The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law

item.title: Data centers are building their own natural gas power plants
item.description:
One of the biggest bottlenecks for new data centers is getting approval to connect to the electric grid — a wait that can last as long as a decade. Some developers are refusing to wait and are instead building their own off-grid, or "behind-the-meter," natural gas power plants to fuel the AI boom, with xAI among the companies pursuing the approach.

The trend underscores how the AI infrastructure race is reshaping energy policy: the demand for compute is so intense that tech companies are becoming power producers in their own right. It also raises questions about emissions and local air quality, since these gas plants can be built faster and with less oversight than grid-scale projects, and communities near them may bear the environmental costs.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
  • MIT Technology Review: The Download: AI’s gas power boom and a consciousness reality check

item.title: Take-Two shuts down fan project to run GTA VI on PC
item.description:
Take-Two has issued a DMCA takedown against Leonida, a fan project aiming to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC by translating a leaked Xbox build. The project, created by 15-year-old developer "NotRexed," has vanished following the notice from GTA VI's publisher.

The takedown is the latest in the race between modding communities and publishers ahead of GTA VI's console launch, with PC players eager to play a game that has no announced PC release date. Take-Two has a long history of aggressively protecting its intellectual property, and the swift action against a high-profile project signals it will not tolerate unofficial PC ports, even ones built from leaked builds.

Sources

  • The Verge: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two

item.title: US Army to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa
item.description:
The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation's stockpile of lead azide — nearly 10,000 pounds of it — at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00 AM CST on Wednesday. Lead azide is a primary explosive used in detonators, and the stockpile has become unstable with age, making controlled destruction the safest option.

The Army has been planning the controlled detonation as a way to eliminate a hazardous stockpile before it poses a greater risk. The Verge is tracking the operation and will keep its coverage updated as the detonation happens and as officials report on the outcome.

Sources

  • The Verge: Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa

item.title: Trump engineered Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
item.description:
Jensen Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, and the comeback was engineered at the highest levels. After the board accepted his resignation following reports of his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — and then a second affair with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him — President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance intervened to make sure he returned. Trump had initially sounded resigned to Huang's exit, saying he would "end up on his feet."

The reinstatement, roughly two weeks after the resignation, stunned most observers and sent the market up. The Verge's commentary frames it as elite impunity: a founder-CEO survives a scandal that would end most executives, with political backing. But the story is not closed — Huang is due to testify before the House on December 1, and investigators are probing alleged chip smuggling to China.

Sources

  • The Verge: Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
  • The Verge: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next?
  • The Verge: Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang

item.title: Kagi takes on Gmail with a privacy-first email service
item.description:
Kagi, the paid search engine that positions itself as a Google alternative, is now taking on Gmail. The company announced a public beta of Kagi Mail, promising "no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in."

It is the latest step in Kagi's strategy of building a paid, privacy-first alternative stack piece by piece: search first, then its Orion browser as a Chrome rival, now email. The bet is that a growing segment of users will pay to escape ad-supported services entirely. Whether email — the stickiest of all Google services — is where that bet pays off remains to be seen, but the beta launch makes Kagi the most complete Google alternative yet.

Sources

  • The Verge: Google alternative Kagi launches an email service

item.title: GTA VI leaker sentenced to seven years — and released
item.description:
Arion Kurtaj, the hacker who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022, years before the game's public release, has been sentenced to seven years in prison — but released on license, according to the BBC. Kurtaj pleaded guilty last week to hacking Rockstar Games as well as Uber and Revolut.

The sentence closes one of the most notorious chapters in gaming history: the 2022 leak was among the largest in the industry and forced Rockstar to confirm the game's existence earlier than planned. Kurtaj's release on license means he serves the sentence in the community under conditions rather than behind bars, a conclusion that will likely draw mixed reactions from the companies he targeted.

Sources

  • The Verge: The hacker behind early GTA VI leaks has been sentenced — and released

item.title: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is ready to test
item.description:
Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. Developer Andreas Kling announced on Monday that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux after more than four years of development.

The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine, rather than a fork of Chromium, WebKit, or Gecko. In a web dominated by a single engine, an independent implementation is a meaningful event for the open web — even in alpha, it gives developers and standards advocates something they have not had in years: a genuinely alternative rendering engine to test against.

Sources

  • The Verge: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test

item.title: AI data centers crash the UN climate talks
item.description:
The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry AI data centers are surging — and that collision dominated the United Nations climate conference, COP31, which closed chaotically in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.

Delegates spent the summit grappling with a paradox: data centers are driving a huge new wave of electricity demand at the very moment countries are supposed to be decarbonizing their grids. The conference ended unsatisfyingly, with the data-center question unresolved. The episode captures a tension that will only grow: AI's appetite for power is now a climate-policy problem, not just a tech-industry one.

Sources

  • The Verge: AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks

item.title: A legendary philosopher isn't buying Anthropic's consciousness argument
item.description:
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for investors — a striking disclosure that raised the profile of a long-running philosophical debate. Now a legendary philosopher is pushing back on the company's framing of model sentience and moral status.

The exchange matters because Anthropic's IPO filing made machine consciousness a matter of securities law, not just seminar-room debate. If a leading AI lab tells investors its systems might be sentient, the question of what that claim means — and what obligations it would create — stops being academic. The philosopher's skepticism is a reminder that the science of consciousness has not settled the question Anthropic is now asking the market to price.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

item.title: Using rocks for carbon removal could eventually hurt crop growth
item.description:
Tech companies are investing heavily in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to startups that spread crushed basalt, olivine, and other alkaline materials across farms to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. The technique, known as enhanced rock weathering, is one of the most popular carbon-removal bets in the industry.

But influential models now suggest a catch: over time, the practice could eventually reduce crop growth. If the carbon-removal method undermines the farms it depends on, the economics and the climate math both change. The finding is a reminder that large-scale geoengineering-style interventions carry second-order effects that only show up at scale.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

item.title: Apple renews Ted Lasso for season 5
item.description:
Apple has renewed Ted Lasso for a fifth season on Apple TV, following what the company calls a "record-breaking season four debut." The show remains one of Apple's biggest, and the renewal keeps it going for at least one more run.

There are no details yet about the new season or when it might debut. The renewal is notable partly because season four was itself a comeback — and its strong debut evidently convinced Apple the show still has an audience worth investing in.

Sources

  • The Verge: Apple renews Ted Lasso for season 5

item.title: A week of major outages — FAA, Outlook, JPMorgan, now Delta — and experts say more are coming
item.description:
It's been a rough stretch for infrastructure. Over the last week or so, the US has seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase — and on Sunday, Delta flights in and out of Atlanta faced significant delays due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane's weight and balance. Atlanta is Delta's largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world.

The consensus among experts is that there are more outages to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN the American people should expect further disruptions. The common thread isn't one cause — it's how much of daily life now runs through a small number of interdependent systems, so when one fails, the blast radius is enormous.

Sources

  • The Verge: We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
  • The Verge: Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage

item.title: Protesters storm Meta's offices in India
item.description:
Members of India's opposition Congress party protested outside Meta's offices in Delhi on Friday and appear to have entered the building in a video shared by CNN. Members of the party's youth wing are demanding the company restore accounts of party leaders and warned of more protests to come.

The Congress party has criticized Meta over account suspensions, and the confrontation puts the company back in the middle of India's charged political environment. Meta's content decisions in India — its largest market by users — keep colliding with the country's politics, and this time the protest came to its doorstep.

Sources

  • The Verge: Protesters storm Meta offices in India

item.title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music after Steam review-bombing
item.description:
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after players discovered that a segment of the game used AI-generated music. A Reddit user found several audio files with Suno metadata in a Grand Theft Auto-themed section of the game — and the community response was swift and negative.

The developer has now removed the AI music. It's the latest example of a pattern: AI-generated assets slipped into a beloved game, players found out, and the backlash forced a reversal. For game studios, the lesson is getting clearer — if you're going to use AI-generated content, players expect to be told upfront.

Sources

  • The Verge: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus

item.title: Switch 2 gets its first Black Friday deal: $50 off the console, $20 off games
item.description:
Nintendo is knocking $50 off a Switch 2 console bundle starting today, November 22, through Saturday, December 5 — giving shoppers plenty of time to think it over after Cyber Monday. It's the first meaningful discount on the console, which has held its price since launch.

Switch 2 games are also getting $20 off some of the best titles, making Black Friday a good moment to expand a new library. If you've been waiting for any reason to pick up the console, this is the first one Nintendo has offered.

Sources

  • The Verge: Nintendo’s Switch 2 console is $50 off for Black Friday
  • The Verge: Some of our favorite Switch 2 games are cheaper through Black Friday

item.title: Kodak's next collectible is a tiny photo frame that doubles as a tracker
item.description:
Reto's follow-up to its tiny Kodak Charmera camera is an equally small digital photo frame you can clip to a keychain — but the Kodak SlideTag goes one step further than its predecessor: it also works as a tracker, compatible with both Apple's Find My and Google's Find Hub networks.

Where the Charmera's usefulness stopped at snapping grainy photos and terrible videos, the SlideTag displays your shots on a tiny e-ink screen and helps you find your keys. It's a collectible first and a practical gadget second, but the tracker integration is a genuinely clever twist on the novelty-camera trend.

Sources

  • The Verge: Kodak’s next collectible is a tiny digital photo frame that doubles as a tracker

item.title: An off-Broadway show where the audience listens on headphones, thanks to Auracast
item.description:
At the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse in New York, ushers hand each audience member a black drawstring bag with wired headphones connected to a small Auracast receiver — and the show's audio comes through the headphones, not the room's speakers.

Auracast, the Bluetooth broadcast standard, lets a venue stream audio directly to many listeners at once. For theater, it means every seat gets the same crisp mix, and it opens the door to assistive listening without special hardware. It's a small production using a new standard in a genuinely thoughtful way — and a glimpse of how live performance audio might work in a few years.

Sources

  • The Verge: ‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’

item.title: FBI and USDA reportedly hacked; NCIC system targeted
item.description:
Both the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the FBI were reportedly hacked on Friday, in separate incidents reported the same day. The FBI breach targeted the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) — the database federal, state, and local law enforcement rely on for criminal records, warrants, and missing-persons information. According to CNN, this is the second attack on the FBI in the last few months.

A breach of the NCIC is serious business: it's the backbone of day-to-day policing across the country, and a compromise there raises questions about data integrity and access control at the bureau. Details on what was taken or how the attackers got in remain sparse, but two federal breaches in one day — and a repeat hit on the FBI — point to a rough week for U.S. government cybersecurity.

Sources

  • The Verge: The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked

item.title: UN talks on 'killer robots' end with no rules agreed
item.description:
A week of UN negotiations in Geneva on rules governing autonomous weapons — so-called "killer robots" — ended without agreement. Diplomats left the meetings having only agreed to "start discussing options," after a largely fruitless round of talks on how, or whether, to regulate weapons systems that can select and engage targets without human intervention.

The failure to agree leaves a widening gap between the technology and the law: autonomous weapons are already being developed and deployed, while the international rules meant to govern them haven't moved past the discussion stage. For now, the only outcome is more talks, with no timeline for binding rules in sight.

Sources

  • The Verge: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’

item.title: Amazon slaps anti-regulation labels on NYC deliveries
item.description:
Amazon is escalating its fight against New York City's Delivery Protection Act by putting labels on shipments warning customers that the City Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The bill would effectively ban the third-party delivery arrangements Amazon currently uses in the city, and the company is now taking its case directly to customers' doorsteps.

The move is a lobbying tactic dressed up as a shipping notice — Amazon is using its own packages as billboards in a regulatory fight. Whether the $5 figure holds up is beside the point for now; the company is clearly willing to spend real political capital to stop a law that would reshape how it delivers in the country's largest market.

Sources

  • The Verge: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too

item.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first after its IPO?
item.description:
Anthropic, the AI lab behind Claude, went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday, and The Verge's latest podcast episode digs into the question hanging over the listing: can a company whose founding identity is built on AI safety keep that promise once it's answering to public shareholders? Senior AI reporter Hayden Field joins to talk through the IPO, the company's unusual governance structure, and the tension between safety commitments and market pressure.

The numbers are gigantic, but the real story is structural — Anthropic is the first major AI lab to test whether a safety-first charter survives the stock market. How it navigates investor demands for growth against its own stated constraints will be a closely watched precedent for the whole AI industry.

Sources

  • The Verge: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?

item.title: Chess.com goes way beyond chess with Classic Games hub
item.description:
Chess.com is expanding well beyond its namesake. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding ten more games — backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called Word — under a new Classic Games platform.

The move turns Chess.com into a broader hub for classic board and puzzle games, leveraging the same audience and infrastructure that made it the dominant chess site. It's a bet that the millions of players who show up for chess will stick around for the rest of the classics, and it positions the company as a general games platform rather than a single-game destination.

Sources

  • The Verge: Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku

item.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro review: two screens still aren't better than one
item.description:
Xiaomi added a second screen to the back of its flagship phones with last year's 17 Pro series, but those never left China — so the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance most reviewers have had to test whether a rear display is actually useful. The verdict, per The Verge's review: it isn't, at least not in a way that justifies the complexity.

The rear screen is a fun idea that keeps running into the same problem as every dual-screen experiment before it: it duplicates things the main screen already does well, without adding a compelling use of its own. For a flagship that will compete on camera and performance anyway, the second screen ends up as a novelty rather than a reason to buy.

Sources

  • The Verge: The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one

item.title: GTA VI made $3.79 billion in its first day — a record for any entertainment
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day of sales, setting what Rockstar calls a new record for entertainment across any medium — not just games, but movies and music too. The game also sold 32.5 million preorder copies before launch.

The scale is hard to overstate: after a 13-year wait, GTA VI didn't just meet expectations, it dwarfed them. Preorders alone were reportedly worth around $1.6 billion. The launch also had a lighter side effect — "GTA Flu" is spreading, with one payroll processor reporting PTO requests up 9% this week. Rockstar's next problem is a good one: keeping the servers and the hype running.

item.title: YouTube is reportedly set to pay $3 billion to settle social media addiction claims
item.description:
YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its "addictive design" harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources say YouTube has reached an agreement in principle, and the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.

The settlement would let Google avoid a wave of litigation from school districts arguing that social media platforms were designed to keep children hooked at the expense of their wellbeing. At $3 billion it's one of the largest settlements of its kind, and the teen safeguards attached to it could matter more in the long run than the money — if they actually change how the platform works for young users.

item.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with Claude's help
item.description:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis — one of mathematics' most notoriously difficult problems, unsolved for 167 years — with the help of Claude. If verified, it would be a seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and would resolve a Millennium Prize problem.

The claim comes with a twist: a competing human proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, by Alessandro Masullo, has also surfaced this week, and mathematicians are now scrutinizing both. Proofs of this magnitude take months or years to verify, so the honest status is "claimed, not confirmed" — but either way, the week has been extraordinary for a problem that has eluded the world's best mathematicians for over a century.

item.title: Trump threatens a 'tremendous tax' on AI data centers built outside the US
item.description:
President Donald Trump promised to put a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers outside the United States, saying "we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country." The threat comes even as states and cities across the US are placing restrictions on new data center applications of their own.

The tension is the story: the administration wants AI infrastructure built domestically, while local communities increasingly push back against the power and water demands of new data centers. A tax on foreign builds would raise the cost of the industry's global expansion — and it's far from clear how it would work in practice, given how intertwined the major cloud providers' international operations are.

  • The Verge: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US

item.title: Google is killing Assistant on smart speakers and shutting down the Nest app
item.description:
Google is making sweeping changes to its smart home software: starting next year, it will retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices, and the Nest app will shut down on January 25, 2027, with management moving to the Google Home app.

It's the end of an era for the Assistant, which once defined Google's smart home ambitions, and a consolidation around Gemini as the company's AI interface everywhere. For Nest owners, the practical message is simple: migrate to the Google Home app before the deadline, because the old app — and the old assistant — are going away whether you're ready or not.

Sources

  • The Verge: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year

item.title: Teenage Engineering's first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
item.description:
Teenage Engineering has announced the EP/BC-1, what it calls "a modern take on a classic CD player" — a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or in a slide-out tray. It's the first entry in the company's new broadcast series.

It's a characteristically Teenage Engineering product: a format most of the industry declared dead, rebuilt as a design object for people who never stopped loving physical media. Whether the CD revival is real or nostalgic, the EP/BC-1 is the most interesting piece of audio hardware in a while — a player that treats the disc itself as part of the show.
